title: Making a French groove case
subtitle: Building a case-bound cover with a recessed hinge groove for a clean opening
excerpt: A French groove is a channel scored into the cover board a few millimetres from the spine, covered over by the cloth or paper covering. When the book opens, it pivots at the groove rather than at the spine itself, which protects the covering material and makes the book easier to open flat.
sourceNotes: Douglas Cockerell, Bookbinding and the Care of Books (1901), chapter on case construction and hinge grooves. The French groove is described as the standard method for producing a clean-opening case-bound book where the book cloth must not crack at the spine edge.

glossaryTerms.definition: A gap between the cover board and the spine piece, formed by setting the boards 3 to 5 mm away from the spine liner when constructing the case. The covering cloth bridges the gap, forming a flexible hinge.
The separate strip of card or thick paper that forms the spine of the case, positioned between the two cover boards when the case is constructed.

in a case-bound cover. The covering cloth bridges the gap, which is covered when the book is closed but opens as a flexible hinge when the book is opened. Without a groove, the cloth cracks at the spine edge over time. The French groove shifts the stress of opening away from the spine covering and onto a shaped gap, which never cracks.

items.name: Bookbinding board, 2 mm, two pieces
items.notes: Cover boards, cut 3 mm larger than the text block on head, tail, and foredge.

items.name: Spine piece: stiff card, 1.5-2 mm
items.notes: A strip cut to the spine width (measured across the rounded-and-backed text block spine) and the height of the text block plus the two board squares.

items.name: Book cloth or covering paper
items.notes: A single piece large enough to cover both boards, spine, and turn-ins with 20 mm spare on each edge.

items.name: Teflon bone folder
items.notes: For rubbing cloth into the French groove without leaving a shine mark.

content.text: Position the boards on the cloth

Lay the covering cloth face-down on a clean surface. Place the spine piece in the centre. Position the front board 4 mm from the spine piece edge (not flush with it). Repeat for the back board on the other side. This 4 mm gap on each side is the French groove channel. Mark the board positions lightly with a pencil. The spine piece and both boards should be parallel, with exactly 4 mm on each side.
Glue the boards to the cloth

Apply thinned PVA to the face-down boards and spine piece with the paste brush. Lower each component carefully onto the cloth at the marked positions. Press each firmly, then turn the whole assembly over and rub through the cloth with the Teflon bone folder to bond every surface. Pay particular attention to the cloth in the French groove channel: use the tip of the folder to press it lightly into the groove without fully closing it. The cloth should bridge the gap cleanly, not sag into it.

Fold the cloth turn-ins over the board edges in the usual sequence: long sides first (head and tail), then the foredge sides. Mitre the corners. Press the completed case under a flat board with heavy weights for two hours. The French groove should be visible as a slight depression on each side of the spine when the case is closed, and should open freely as a pivot line when the case is opened.

items.symptom: The groove disappears when the cloth dries, leaving the board flush against the spine piece
items.cause: The boards were positioned too close to the spine piece (less than 3 mm).
items.fix: The standard groove is 4 mm for a 2 mm board. If the finished case is already dry, the groove cannot be reopened easily. Re-cut the case.

items.symptom: The cloth cracks along the groove line when the case is opened
items.cause: The cloth is too stiff (heavy canvas) or the groove is too narrow.
items.fix: Use a lighter cloth (125 gsm book cloth rather than heavy canvas) and widen the groove to 5 mm. Linen-backed Japanese papers also work better than stiff cloth in narrow grooves.
